items.quote: Of that one onely chiefe Medicine of the most Ancient Phylosophers
items.what: that one onely chiefe Medicine of the most Ancient Phylosophers
items.note: The chapter heading sets apart one single chief Medicine and assigns it to the most ancient philosophers.

items.quote: that chief and universal Phylosophical Phisick
items.what: that chief and universal Phylosophical Phisick
items.note: The chapter's subject is named again as one universal philosophical physic, which Croll says he will now supply.

items.quote: this most secret Secret of secret Secrets
items.note: The same thing is called the most secret of secrets; the text heaps the word to mark it as hidden above all else.

items.quote: the Plannets of inferior Astronomy, whose imperfection and drosse it causeth to vanish
items.note: Planets of an 'inferior Astronomy' have dross and imperfection that the medicine removes; the parenthesis that follows names 'metallick and Humane bodies'. Interpreted (mine): the planets here are earthly bodies, most narrowly the metallic bodies the parenthesis names; the text does not state the equation itself.

items.quote: it segregateth all extraneous Sulphureity and impure Terrestreity from metallick and Humane bodies
items.note: What the medicine does: it separates foreign sulphureity and impure earthiness from metallic and human bodies alike.

items.quote: the recovering covering and preserving of the languishing and lost health of the Human body, by its fiery vigour
items.note: Croll states the medicine restores and preserves human health, by a 'fiery vigour'. The doubled 'recovering covering' stands so in the text.

items.quote: the Gonetick influence of the beames of the Sun and Moon and the fourth revolution is finisht upon its native Earth
items.note: A condition for its 'Magicall and super Celestial use': the generative influence of Sun and Moon's beams and a fourth revolution completed upon 'its native Earth'. The lines do not say what the revolution or the native earth are.

items.quote: it is endowed absolutly with all created Influentiall power as well in the Elementall world, as in the Celestiall or super celestiall
items.note: Once that revolution is finished, the thing is said to hold all created influential power in the elemental, celestial and super-celestial worlds.

items.quote: so doth he usually hide his wonderfull Gifts in wonderfull men
items.note: God is said to hide his wonderful gifts in wonderful men: the gift is lodged in persons, not openly given.

items.quote: All antiquity, also all Verity of all Nations and Languages in the tradition of this doctrine
items.note: Croll appeals to the agreement of all antiquity and all nations' tradition, and to 'ocular inspectation' by many of his own time, as witness that the medicine is real.

items.quote: woven of so many Hieroglyphicall, Magicall, and Mathematicall Coverings
items.note: The writings of the learned are said to be woven of hieroglyphical, magical and mathematical coverings: their truth is given under covers.

items.quote: This occult Minerva of Phylosophy & this only most precious Jewell is inestimable.
items.what: This occult Minerva of Phylosophy & this only most precious Jewell
items.note: The margin names the medicine an occult Minerva of philosophy and the one precious jewel; 'occult' marks it hidden.

items.quote: John Dee of London
items.name: John Dee of London
items.note: Beside the claim of the thing's all-embracing influential power, the margin sends the reader to a writing of John Dee of London (its title partly illegible, 'Mo...ade').

items.quote: and Roger Bacon
items.name: Roger Bacon
items.note: Roger Bacon is named in the same margin note as a further authority for that passage.

items.quote: doth warrant and assure a removall of old age and renewing of youth, perpetuall health, and honest food and rayment
items.note: Croll states what the gift assures its holders: removal of old age, renewed youth, lasting health, and honest food and clothing.

items.quote: to the Pious and holy Phylosophers dignified by Nature and Education
items.note: The benefits are assured only to pious, holy philosophers fitted by nature and education: meant for some only.

items.quote: not by usury and fraud, nor cheating wares, nor by oppression of the poor (as most of our rich men are now inriched) but by industry of work and labour of the hands
items.note: The living it gives comes by handwork, set against usury, fraud and oppression by which, Croll says, most rich men of his day grow rich.

items.quote: God forbid therefore, that, sleighting the example of the Ancients, I should either deny such precious Wonders of GOD
items.note: Croll refuses to deny these wonders or to revile them as idle speculation or dreams, as most do.

items.quote: Those therefore that revile and are ignorant of these divine Banquets, whom the Phylosophers call fools, are not to be admitted to them
items.note: Those who revile or do not know the 'divine Banquets' are to be kept out; the gift is called a banquet and its access is restricted.

items.quote: whom the Phylosophers call fools
items.name: Phylosophers
items.note: The name 'fools' for the scorners is given to the philosophers.

items.quote: whether trusting to my own ingenuity I dare boast also of the preparation hereof in this place
items.note: Croll raises whether he will here claim the preparation of the medicine; the following paragraphs answer by declining to falsify, and the margin casts him only as a pointer of the way.

items.quote: as those covètous Mountebanks and greedy Phylosophists use to doe
items.note: Boasting full knowledge of the Art is what covetous mountebanks and 'Phylosophists' do; Croll sets himself apart from them.

items.quote: Here I would be taken as an Index, or as one standing at the door to direct others the way they should goe
items.note: In the margin Croll names his own role here: a pointer or doorkeeper showing others the way, and a whetstone to spur them, rather than one who claims the Art.

items.quote: because I promised the Courteous Reader a little before, that I would set down at least those things which I had made tryall of
items.note: Points back to an earlier promise in this writing to set down only what he had tried.

items.quote: to falsifie any thing concerning the undoubted certainty of this matter
items.note: Croll says he would not falsify anything about the matter's certainty; he calls the matter 'undoubted'.

items.quote: this Sacred and Divine Art and Science, not of Sophisters, but Phylosophers
items.what: this Sacred and Divine Art and Science
items.note: The Art is named sacred and divine and assigned to philosophers, not 'Sophisters'.

items.quote: none aboundeth with so many Imposters as this
items.note: Croll grants that of all arts this one has the most impostors, while holding it true.

items.quote: it cannot be that a poor or covetous man should spend his time in the study of Phylosophy
items.note: The true seekers are furnished with food and clothing; a poor or covetous man cannot pursue the study.

items.quote: after the example of Solomon, not for wealth, but wisdome
items.name: Solomon
items.note: The seekers pray as Solomon did, for wisdom not wealth, that God open 'the Magazine of Divine knowledge'.

items.quote: the Magazine of Divine knowledge
items.note: Knowledge is set as a store-house that God opens to those who pray.

items.quote: who measure their happinesse at least by Heaven, and the Love of God the giver of every good thing
items.note: One mark of the true seekers: they measure happiness by heaven and the love of God.

items.quote: moved and spurred on to search it out by the love of Secrets and of Nature, according to the Divine Grace
items.note: Another mark: love of secrets and of nature, under divine grace, moves them.

items.quote: doe in the fear of God refuse no honest, constant and possible labor of the hands
items.note: Another mark: seeking knowledge without hope of gain or vainglory, they refuse no honest, constant handwork.

items.quote: By Wisdome the heart is made constant.
items.note: Margin beside the demand for constant labour: wisdom makes the heart constant.

items.quote: to that End which belongs to the Master of Nature, to wit, the Praise and Honour of God, and the good of his needy neighbor
items.note: The last mark: they use the gifts only for God's praise and the neighbour's good; the text glosses 'that End' itself with 'to wit'.

items.quote: in a constant Taciturnity, without pride, which provoketh the envy of all men
items.note: The gift is to be used in lasting silence, without the pride that stirs envy.

items.quote: the Children of the golden doctrine (whose gold is the Omnipotent God)
items.note: Stated: the text glosses the 'gold' of the golden doctrine as God himself, so 'golden' here is not said plainly of metal.

items.quote: is justly and of right to be searched out for the health sake of men
items.note: The rare good is to be sought for men's health.

items.quote: leaving the mettalls to those who with an impious hunger, and a thirsty and insatiable desire of being rich
items.note: The seekers leave 'the mettalls' to those who hunger for riches and torment themselves night and day at risk of body and soul.

items.quote: They that carry about their Treasure and use it publickly. Job 22.25.
items.name: Job
items.note: The margin beside this paragraph speaks of those who carry their treasure about and use it publicly, citing Job 22.25.

items.quote: A Phylosopher must covet Nothing but Wisdome, which is conversant about Divine things
items.note: Croll's rule: the philosopher desires only wisdom about divine things, never riches, and delights in the mysteries of nature.

items.quote: he that is adept or hath attained the same may carry about with him in his purse, not the worth of one Kingdom only, but the wealth almost of the whole World
items.note: The one who has attained it can carry almost the whole world's wealth in his purse, though he does not seek riches.

items.quote: either by the immediate inspiration of the most High, or by the expert ocular demonstration of a wise Master in this Art
items.note: The gift is gained in two ways only: direct inspiration from God, or a wise master's demonstration seen with the eyes; not by wrath or force.

items.quote: That without all controversie this is so, no man that doth apply himselfe to Phylosophy will deny.
items.note: Croll holds that no student of philosophy denies this.

items.quote: passe thorow the porch and gate of the Heavens into the Oratory or Chappell of Apollo, and get to the top of the mount of Chymistry
items.note: Attaining the knowledge is put as a passage through the gate of the heavens into Apollo's chapel and up the mount of Chemistry; the figures are not explained in these lines.

items.quote: who durst lend a hand to another herein, except he hat for a long time, and by much experience known him
items.note: No one dares help another to the secret unless long experience has shown him eminent in fear of God, holiness of life and faith.

items.quote: pure and Harpocraticall Faith
items.note: The faith required is called 'Harpocraticall'. Interpreted (mine): it joins the demand of 'constant Taciturnity' in CH6.10; the lines do not explain the word.

items.quote: But where is that Aegyptian Bird to be found, that we may commend such a Phaenix?
items.note: The worthy pupil is called an Egyptian bird, a phoenix, i.e. one hardly to be found.

items.quote: See Paracel. in his fragments of Physick, which are to be refer'd to the 4 Tome fol. 311.
items.name: Paracel.
items.note: The margin points to Paracelsus's fragments of physic, fourth tome, folio 311, beside this passage.

items.quote: that hath the Secret, & teacheth it while he liveth
items.note: Entrance is only by divine revelation or by word of mouth (printed 'month') from one who has the Secret and teaches it in his lifetime.

items.quote: There is no perfection of things without the help of Divinity, and its demonstration.
items.note: No thing is perfected without divine help and its demonstration.

items.quote: He that desireth this Art, must not be a slave to other mens judgment, nor live upon their purse, and must retire himselfe
items.note: The seeker must be independent in judgment and means and withdraw from company.

items.quote: Too much acquantance hinder them / Who labour to find out this Gem.
items.note: A verse couplet: many acquaintances hinder the search; the thing sought is called a Gem.

items.quote: Praebet amicorum, nil nisi copia damnum.
items.note: A Latin line in the margin beside the couplet, giving the same point: a crowd of friends brings only harm. No speaker is named.

items.quote: doth hinder and much disturb the effect in any operation
items.note: The ill dispositions of a companion (arrogance, incredulity, envy, infidelity) are said to hinder the effect of an operation.

items.quote: Reverend antiquity, with one consent acknowledgeth that never any from the first man to the last could find ont the Divine secreu of that Art
items.name: Reverend antiquity
items.note: Antiquity is made to witness that no one ever found the Art by natural wit, reason or experience.

items.quote: it is somthing Divine and hid, and that which is above Reason
items.note: The secret is called divine, hidden, and above reason.

items.quote: those who have labored and toyled to find out this knowledg by dayly reading and comparing of Authors, do witnesse
items.note: The long toil of those who read and compare authors daily is offered as proof that reading alone does not find it.

items.quote: the glorious God and most blessed bestower of all graces hath reavealed and made it plaine to his faithfull wise ones
items.note: God has revealed it plainly to his faithful wise ones who fear him, that they may praise him.

items.quote: Ecclesiastic. 38.
items.name: Ecclesiastic.
items.note: Scripture cited beside the claim that God revealed it to those who fear him.

items.quote: when men seek the Kingdome of God, and study to finde out the Celestiall Stone in the last place
items.note: The thing is named the Celestial Stone; it is to be sought only after the Kingdom of God.

items.quote: there is not one to whom the doors of Nature are unlockt, and that hath the Divine bolt removed
items.note: Among thousands of seekers hardly one finds Nature's doors unlocked; God's will keeps the bolt in place.

items.quote: it is not expedient for all to their salvation, that they should have Honors & riches with their health
items.note: God withholds it because honours and riches with health would not serve every man's salvation.

items.quote: The one only and true way to all Secrets is to have recourse to God the author of all good
items.note: The only way to all secrets is recourse to God.

items.quote: because the Gate was bolted, that is, the Divine Grace and Benediction was denyed and did resist
items.note: Stated: the text itself glosses the bolted gate as divine grace and blessing withheld.

items.quote: the key of the Phylosophicall Garden (as I know some that have)
items.what: the key of the Phylosophicall Garden
items.note: Some may hold the key of the philosophical garden, and Croll says he knows some who have, yet without grace they cannot enter or gather the fruits of 'the Hermetick Tree'.

items.quote: having got the most true Phylosophycall Ferment or Leaven (but prepar'd by others) have not been able to improve or multiply it any further
items.note: A named stage: a philosophical ferment or leaven, which is to be improved or multiplied; impostors holding one prepared by others could not, for ignorance of 'the principle or beginning'.

items.quote: This is that work that is hid under the robe of the Phylosophicall Virgin, which even one brother would not teach another
items.note: The work is hidden under the robe of the philosophical virgin and not taught even between brothers.

items.quote: it is to no purpose to tempt an Adept Phylosopher with promises of rewards
items.note: No reward or favour moves an adept to part with it.

items.quote: which even one brother would not teach another
items.note: Here no one would teach it even to a brother; CH6.12 names a wise master's ocular demonstration as one way to gain it, and N258 entrance by word of mouth from one who teaches it while he lives.

items.quote: This is that Secret laid up and buryed in the most secret Treasury of the Mind and Memory
items.note: The secret is kept in mind and memory, not elsewhere.

items.quote: doe study and strive to be harsh and rugged, least they should disclose their more abstruse or dark sence to any
items.note: The more occult philosophers write harshly on purpose so as not to disclose their dark sense, not to cast the gem to swine.

items.quote: have in a wise and ingenious craft covenanted and sworn they would never write it plainly in any Book
items.note: The philosophers are said to have sworn never to write it plainly in any book.

items.quote: made it known to any but such who had an understanding allegorically
items.note: It has been made known only to those who understand allegorically.

items.quote: they should also have power to dispence or give Names at their pleasure
items.note: The philosophers claim liberty to give names as they please and to 'cloath their children as they listed': the text says their names are not plain.

items.quote: in their precepts, as in a glasse, it hath been sufficiently made known to men of a wise understanding
items.note: The precepts show it as in a glass, sufficiently, but only to the wise chosen of God and sworn in the Art.

items.quote: Neverthelesse religously affirming, that none can attaine the desired end
items.name: True Phylosophers
items.note: The true philosophers are reported as affirming the condition that follows.

items.quote: though they sleight all particulars, which naturally doe altogether want the virtue of tincturing, unlesse they proceed from the first fountaine
items.note: Particulars lack the power of tincturing unless they come from 'the first fountaine'.

items.quote: before the fat or blood of the Sun and the Dew of the Lunary, be joyned into one body by the circular wheel of the Elements with the help of Art and Nature in the form of an Hexagon
items.note: The one operation the chapter states: the fat or blood of the Sun and the dew of the Lunary joined into one body by the circular wheel of the elements, by art and nature, in the form of a hexagon. The lines do not say what these names stand for.

items.quote: which can never be done except the most High God please
items.note: That joining cannot happen unless God wills it; the gift is of the Holy Spirit.

items.quote: for the Spirit proceedeth from Grace, who inspireth whom he will
items.note: Whoever God denies cannot gain it by any art.

items.quote: God would not manifest this knowledg to all, to avoyd offence.
items.note: The margin gives God's reason for the concealment: to avoid offence.

items.quote: This is not believed, but being proved with the gain of labor, toyl and hazard, it is made plain toward the end which proveth the work.
items.note: The thing is not believed until proved by labour, and becomes plain at the end that proves the work.

items.quote: On this the hinge of the whole busines turneth, as Gold animated by the Salt of Niture is made the chief subject of the Phylosophers metallick Physicks
items.what: the chief subject of the Phylosophers metallick Physicks
items.note: The margin names a chief subject: gold animated by 'the Salt of Niture' (so spelled), and calls this the hinge of the whole business.

items.quote: Gold animated by the Salt of Niture is made the chief subject of the Phylosophers metallick Physicks
items.note: The margin puts gold at the centre of the philosophers' metallic physic, while CH6.11 has the seekers leave 'the mettalls' to the greedy. Several readings: CH6.11 may concern seeking metals for wealth only; the lines do not settle it.

items.quote: Read Gen. 1.27, 28.
items.name: Gen.
items.note: Scripture cited beside the joining 'in the form of an Hexagon'.

items.quote: Hermes his Table
items.name: Hermes
items.note: Hermes's Table is named beside the same passage.

items.quote: Morienes, Alan. Rodargir. Monad.
items.name: Morienes
items.note: Morienes, Alan., Rodargir. and a 'Monad.' are listed as further authorities beside the passage.

items.quote: Lull.
items.name: Lull.
items.note: Lull. closes the list of names, after a partly illegible 'T...evisan.'.

items.quote: Seeing therefore all mans endeavor is but vaine except God prosper it
items.note: All human effort is vain unless God prospers it.

items.quote: Levit. 26.20.
items.name: Levit.
items.note: Scripture cited beside the claim that endeavour is vain without God.

items.quote: wasting their time and estates, should suffer themselves to be cheated and deceived, with the greedy world by the golden promises of circumforaneous, vitious, and most lying Impostors
items.note: Croll wonders that great men of his age let wandering impostors cheat them of time and estates.

items.quote: no perfect perception of Mysteries can be attained to
items.note: Without the liberal and noble arts, which the 'Phylosophists and Imposters' lack, the mysteries cannot be perceived.

items.quote: Great men commit great errours. Psal. 25.14. Prov. 3.32. Wisd. 1.4. Eccl. 43.32, 33.
items.name: Psal.
items.note: A margin saying and scripture citations beside the great men who are deceived.

items.quote: Those Gymnosophists with their Fantasticall and Frantick inventions
items.note: The impostors are named 'Gymnosophists', who enrich ears and empty pockets.

items.quote: whose company we should avoyd even as the most raging torments of hell
items.note: Croll's counsel: shun the impostors' company.

items.quote: the Wisdome of the Lord, whose mysterie is onely with them that Fear him
items.note: The mystery is with those who fear God only and does not enter wicked souls.

items.quote: with their guilfull devices of painting white and red, and pargetting womens faces
items.note: The impostors have deceived the world with devices of painting white and red and plastering women's faces. The lines read plainly as cosmetics; any further sense is not stated.

items.quote: Great gaine is the scope of sophisticall craft, because Dust & Ashes is the end of such smock-sellers.
items.note: The margin says sophistical craft aims at gain and ends in dust and ashes.

items.quote: playing away and losing the story of Pandora
items.note: The impostors are said to lose 'the story of Pandora'; the lines do not explain the figure.

items.quote: what Alphidius foretold should happen to them
items.name: Alphidius
items.note: Alphidius is given the prophecy of what the impostors find.

items.quote: instead of the Tincture they should find only the colour, instead of the Hermetick Stone a pibble or glasse
items.note: Alphidius's words set the true things (the Tincture, the Hermetic Stone, treasure) against what the impostors get (colour, pebble or glass, coals and ashes).

items.quote: this efficacious transmutatory virtue of these Impostors, which makes wise men fools, strong men weak, rich men poor
items.note: Ironical: the only 'transmutatory virtue' the impostors have is to change wise men into fools and rich men into beggars.

items.quote: Piety is the most necessary key to the knowledge of all Secrets.
items.note: Piety is called the key to all secrets.

items.quote: See Rodargirus BRITTO SARMATUS his verse
items.name: Rodargirus BRITTO SARMATUS
items.note: The margin points to a verse of Rodargirus Britto Sarmatus against those who rush into 'the Vestry of Phylosophy'.

items.quote: It is not expedient to reveal it to any carnall man, because thou wilt be accuised for making known so great a Secret.
items.note: It must not be revealed to the carnal; the revealer is cursed ('accuised' as printed).

items.quote: He that publisheth this Art, let him die an evill death, saith Lully
items.name: Lully
items.note: Lully is quoted cursing whoever publishes the Art, because God alone reveals it.

items.quote: because it is a secret to be given and revealed by God alone who hath created Nature
items.note: Only God reveals it, to whom he will.

items.quote: the envy of Phylosophers is not against the Children of Art and Science, who seek not their own but Gods glory
items.note: The philosophers' 'envy' is not aimed at worthy seekers who seek God's glory.

items.quote: after he by the Blessing of God hath happily labored like Hermes more then twenty years
items.note: The adept is pictured as having laboured, like Hermes, more than twenty years.

items.quote: will be lesse afraid to die an hundred most cruell deaths, and indure all manner of miseries and punishment
items.note: The adept would rather die a hundred deaths than publish the treasure to the wicked or unworthy.

items.quote: this greatest and richest Terrene Treasure, the Perfect Benefit or good gift of GOD
items.what: this greatest and richest Terrene Treasure
items.note: The secret is named the greatest earthly treasure and God's perfect gift.

items.quote: which Secret would by evill men, with the ruine of the whole world, be abused
items.note: Reason for keeping it: in evil hands it would ruin the world.

items.quote: except he can give a good account of his Stewardship and the Talent committed to him
items.note: The adept is a steward who must answer to God's judgment for the talent entrusted.

items.quote: the heat of the Centre united to the heat of Sun shall set all corruption of the Elements on fire
items.note: At the last day the heat of the centre joined to the sun's heat will burn all corruption of the elements.

items.quote: when every evill and impure thing shall be cast like lead with the damned into Hell
items.note: The impure is cast like lead into hell, burning there 'like molten glasse' without wasting.

items.quote: The property of fire is to seperate the impurity of the Elements.
items.note: The margin states fire's property: to separate impurity from the elements, in line with the purging said of the medicine in CH6.1.

items.quote: Read Isa. Holand in opere minerali.
items.name: Isa. Holand
items.note: The margin points to Isa. Holand's mineral work beside the passage on the world's end by fire.

items.quote: Apoc. 20.10. The end of the world is by fire. There is a Sea of glass mingled with fire. Apoc. 15.2.
items.name: Apoc.
items.note: Scripture cited for the end of the world by fire and a sea of glass mingled with fire.
